biological.citation: G protein pathway suppressor 2 suppresses aerobic glycolysis through RACK1-mediated HIF-1α degradation in breast cancer. (PMID: 38942092)
biological.summary: GPS2 suppresses aerobic glycolysis in breast cancer cells by destabilizing HIF-1α, reducing transcription of downstream glycolytic regulators (PGK1, PGAM1, ENO1, PKM2, LDHA, PDK1/2/4). GPS2 directly binds RACK1 via its N-terminal residues 70-92 aa, stabilizing the HIF-1α/RACK1 interaction and promoting HIF-1α polyubiquitination and degradation. GPS2 is low-expressed in breast cancer tissues and negatively correlated with poor prognosis.
biological.sample_size: 21 BC cases plus in vitro/in vivo models

biological.citation: Liquid-liquid phase separation of GPS2-LATS1 promotes colorectal cancer progression by reprogramming lipid metabolism. (PMID: 40715488)
biological.summary: GPS2 is overexpressed in colorectal cancer and acts as an oncogenic driver by undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via its coiled-coil domain. Phase-separated GPS2 interacts with the kinase domain of LATS1, inducing LATS1 LLPS and suppressing its activity, thereby releasing YAP to amplify SREBP1/PPARα-driven lipid metabolism. GPS2 depletion inhibits tumor growth in vitro and in vivo, while overexpression accelerates malignancy.

biological.citation: Inhibition of K63 ubiquitination by G-Protein pathway suppressor 2 (GPS2) regulates mitochondria-associated translation. (PMID: 39094987)
biological.summary: GPS2 inhibits non-proteolytic K63 ubiquitination mediated by the E2 enzyme Ubc13, with targets enriched for RNA-binding and translation proteins on the outer mitochondrial membrane, including PABPC1, RPS1, RACK1, and eIF3M. Removal of GPS2-mediated inhibition (via genetic deletion or stress-induced nuclear translocation) promotes import-coupled translation of selected mRNAs, increasing expression of an adaptive antioxidant program. This reveals GPS2 as a regulator of nuclear-mitochondria communication through spatially coordinated transcription and translation.

biological.citation: Antagonistic action of GPS2 and KDM1A at enhancers governs alternative macrophage activation by interleukin 4. (PMID: 36610795)
biological.summary: GPS2, as a core subunit of the HDAC3/SMRT/NCOR corepressor complex, represses IL4-dependent enhancer activation in mouse macrophages by antagonizing the lysine demethylase KDM1A (LSD1). Corepressor depletion increased KDM1A recruitment to enhancers of IL4-induced genes, causing demethylation of repressive H3K9me2/3 marks and enhancer/gene activation even in the absence of IL4/STAT6. This identifies a novel epigenetic corepressor-coactivator switching mechanism governing alternative macrophage activation.

biological.citation: GPS2 promotes erythroid differentiation by control of the stability of EKLF protein. (PMID: 32384137)
biological.summary: GPS2 interacts with the erythroid transcription factor EKLF/KLF1 and prevents its proteasome-mediated degradation, thereby increasing EKLF stability and transcriptional activity. Knockdown of GPS2 significantly suppresses erythroid differentiation of human CD34+ cells in vitro and in xenotransplantation models, and global GPS2 deletion in mice causes impaired fetal liver erythropoiesis and severe anemia. The GPS2-binding region maps to amino acids 191-230 of EKLF, which is highly conserved in mammals.

biological.citation: GPS2 regulates embryonic angiogenesis by enhancing endothelial cell survival through stabilizing HOIP. (PMID: 41507360)
biological.summary: EC-specific GPS2 knockout mice (Gps2ECKO) are embryonic lethal at E16.5 due to defective vascularization caused by aberrant TNFR1-mediated endothelial cell death. GPS2 binds the NZF domain of HOIP and inhibits K48-linked polyubiquitination at K579, K737, and K988, preventing HOIP proteasomal degradation and maintaining LUBAC stability and NF-κB activation. TNFR1 deletion in Gps2ECKO mice restores normal vascularization and rescues embryonic lethality.

biological.citation: GPS2 confers l-asparaginase resistance in acute lymphoblastic leukemia cells through ATF4/ASNS axis. (PMID: 40693356)
biological.summary: GPS2 binds ATF4 and stabilizes it by impairing the interaction between ATF4 and the E3 ligase BTRC, thereby inhibiting ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of ATF4 and upregulating downstream asparagine synthetase (ASNS). GPS2 knockdown sensitizes ALL cells to l-asparaginase treatment in vitro and increases l-ASP efficacy against xenografted ALL tumors in vivo. These findings identify GPS2 as a positive regulator of the ATF4/ASNS axis conferring chemotherapy resistance.

biological.citation: Recurrent FOXK1::GRHL and GPS2::GRHL fusions in trichogerminoma. (PMID: 35049062)
biological.summary: RNA sequencing of trichogerminoma tumors identified recurrent in-frame GPS2::GRHL1, GPS2::GRHL2, and GPS2::GRHL3 fusion transcripts in 4 of 21 cases, alongside FOXK1::GRHL1/2 fusions. These gene fusions were not detected in other follicular tumor entities or basal cell carcinomas, suggesting GRHL gene rearrangements (including GPS2 as a fusion partner) may be the oncogenic driver in this subset of follicular tumors. The GPS2::GRHL fusions were validated by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq.

biological.citation: Inherited Thrombocytopenia Related Genes: GPS2 Mediates the Interplay Between ANKRD26 and ETV6. (PMID: 39791724)
biological.summary: GPS2, as a component of the NCoR complex, binds both ANKRD26 and ETV6, mediating their interaction and contributing to cytoplasmic retention of ETV6. ANKRD26 overexpression deregulates ETV6 transcriptional repression, and GPS2 is identified as the molecular bridge in a novel ANKRD26-ETV6-GPS2 axis relevant to inherited thrombocytopenias with predisposition to myeloid neoplasms. This provides mechanistic insight into how mutations in ANKRD26 may phenocopy ETV6-related thrombocytopenia.

biological.citation: GPS2-mediated regulation of the adipocyte secretome modulates adipose tissue remodeling at the onset of diet-induced obesity. (PMID: 36731652)
biological.summary: Adipocyte-specific GPS2 knockout (GPS2-AKO) mice fed a high-fat diet are significantly more inflamed, insulin resistant, and obese compared to wild-type counterparts, demonstrating GPS2's role in metabolic adaptation. Loss of GPS2 in adipocytes alters the exosomal secretome, promoting a TGFβ-driven fibrotic microenvironment and anti-adipogenic stromal cell composition. Single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomics revealed that GPS2 regulates intercellular communication between adipocytes and stromal cells during early obesity.
